clue.text: South African leader bleats

definitions.meaning: an Afrikaans word for a master or boss, used in South Africa
the cries a sheep makes, as a plural noun

explanation.definitionFit: Baas is the Afrikaans term for a boss, and baas is also the written cry of sheep.

clue.text: Coin to chuck? Not good when it contains gold

indicators.note: when it contains says the shortened word is wrapped round the next piece
Not tells us the letter for good is to be dropped from the word

parts.note: to chuck something is to fling it
OR is the heraldic term for gold

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether to toss a coin away, unless it has gold in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chuck' reads as a verb about the coin, but it is the synonym source; 'Not good' and 'when it contains' then trim and wrap it, leaving FLIN around the gold.
explanation.definitionFit: The florin was an old British two-shilling coin, worth ten pence after decimalisation.

clue.text: What is a prime bit of the best all-night ice verse conjured up?

definitions.text: What is a prime bit of the best all-night ice verse conjured up?

indicators.note: conjured up suggests the letters are magicked into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, part of the letters to rearrange

indicators.note: the prime bit of a word is its opening letter, so only that letter of the word the is used

parts.note: taken as written, the rest of the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A riddle asking which line of poetry is the finest about a freezing night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conjured up' rearranges WHATISA, T (first letter of 'the') and BESTALLNIGHTICEVERSE, 28 letters, into the opening line of Keats's poem The Eve of St Agnes, which is indeed icy verse about one long night.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats's The Eve of St Agnes begins with this line, describing a bitterly cold night, so it is a prime piece of icy verse.

clue.text: Body discovered outside University College in Oxford

indicators.note: discovered outside says the first word is found wrapped around the next letter

parts.note: a corps is an organised body of people

explanation.surface: A dead body turns up just outside a university college in Oxford.
explanation.definitionFit: Corpus Christi is one of the colleges of Oxford University, usually called by its first word.

clue.text: Grass, full of hypocrisy, renounced former practice

indicators.note: full of says the grass word holds the next piece inside it

parts.note: a reed is a tall grass
cant is insincere, hypocritical talk

explanation.surface: An informer, steeped in hypocrisy, gives up their old habits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' looks like an informer here, but it is the plant REED.
explanation.definitionFit: To recant is to take back a belief or practice publicly, so renounced former practice is a fair paraphrase.

clue.text: Proceed to first item on agenda — Minutes

parts.note: to act is to proceed or take action

indicators.note: the first item on a word is its opening letter, here of agenda

explanation.surface: A chairperson moves the meeting to item one, the minutes.
explanation.definitionFit: Acta is a Latin-derived term for official records or proceedings, in effect the minutes of a meeting.

clue.text: Earnest raising of hat when meeting one distinguished fellow

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising the word means reading it from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: a lid is slang for a hat
I is the Roman numeral for one
a gent is a gentleman, a distinguished fellow

explanation.surface: Someone sincerely raises their hat on meeting an eminent man.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'raising of' turns the hat word upward, giving DIL; 'when meeting' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Diligent means hard-working and conscientious, which is close to earnest.

clue.text: House is virtuous, no drug being found

indicators.note: no says the drug letter is absent from the word

parts.note: clean can mean morally pure or virtuous
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A household is respectable because no drugs are found there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House' is a family line, as in the House of Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: A noble house is a family line, and a clan is likewise an extended family group.

clue.text: Differing form for scientists showing grant — something binding?

parts.note: to allot is to grant or assign
a rope is something used to tie or bind

explanation.surface: Researchers are shown a grant, apparently with strings attached.
explanation.definitionFit: Chemists call each different structural form of the same element, such as diamond and graphite, by this term.

clue.text: See 3
Shoot in due season, new to emerge

indicators.note: to emerge says the letter for new comes out of the season word

parts.note: spring is the season when new growth is due

explanation.surface: A young shoot appears at the proper time of year.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprig is a small shoot or twig of a plant.

clue.text: Scheme laid down by heretic, a sort of worm

parts.note: a plan is a scheme
an Arian followed Arius, whose teaching the early Church condemned as heresy

explanation.surface: A heretic lays down a plan, which turns out to be a kind of worm.
explanation.definitionFit: Planarians are small flatworms often studied for their power to regrow.

clue.text: Crazy types getting huge bonuses should receive nothing (not ace!)

indicators.note: should receive says the shortened word takes the next letter inside
not says the letter for ace is removed

parts.note: bankers are notorious for their large bonuses
A is the abbreviation for ace in cards
O is a zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A grumble that people paid enormous bonuses ought to get nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not ace' takes A from BANKERS, leaving BNKERS; 'should receive' puts O inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Bonkers is informal British slang for mad or crazy.

clue.text: John, useless dud

parts.note: john is US slang for a toilet, and bog is British slang for one
US is shorthand for useless, from the Latin-style abbreviation used in British slang

explanation.surface: A man named John is dismissed as a useless failure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'John' looks like a name; it is a toilet, and BOG is the British slang equivalent.
explanation.definitionFit: Bogus means fake, and a dud is something fake or worthless.

clue.text: Be ill, held by nurse? There's nothing after this

indicators.note: held by says the first piece sits inside the next

parts.note: to tend a patient is to nurse them
to ail is to be ill

explanation.surface: A sick patient is cared for by a nurse, with a hint that this is the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The tail end is the very last part of something, with nothing following it.

clue.text: Arsonist in church with name put on record

parts.note: CE stands for the Church of England
a diary is a daily record

explanation.surface: A fire-raiser in church has his name put on file.
explanation.definitionFit: An incendiary is a person who deliberately starts fires, the same as an arsonist.

clue.text: Maybe disco gate's sealed off at ten

indicators.note: sealed off says those letters are shut off from the word

parts.note: gate is the number attending a sports match, its attendance; the 's reads as is
taken as written, the letters removed

explanation.surface: A disco shuts its gates at ten o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: In British sport a match's 'gate' is the attendance; remove ATTEN to leave the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A disco is one example of a dance, an event for dancing, hence the maybe.

clue.text: Wine running short? That's serious

indicators.note: running short says the wine's name loses its last letter

parts.note: Graves is a wine from the Bordeaux region of France

explanation.surface: Running out of wine is no laughing matter.
explanation.definitionFit: Grave as an adjective means serious or solemn.

clue.text: See 3
Hero who may track down criminals?

definitions.meaning: El ..., the medieval Spanish champion, is a national hero
the Criminal Investigation Department of British police, the detectives

explanation.definitionFit: El Cid was the Castilian warrior hero, and CID is the British police detective branch.

clue.text: Thief is a great evil — put criminal inside

indicators.note: inside says the rearranged letters go within the evil word

parts.note: a curse is a great evil or affliction

indicators.note: criminal suggests the following letters are twisted out of order

explanation.surface: A thief is declared a great evil and told to be locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'criminal' makes TPU from the word 'put', and 'inside' sets it in the great evil; 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A cutpurse was an old word for a pickpocket, a thief who cut purse strings.

clue.text: Copper — idiot about to drive dangerously?

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

indicators.note: about indicates the word for idiot is turned round

parts.note: a nit is a fool

explanation.surface: A police officer calls someone an idiot for reckless driving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' looks like a policeman; it is the metal. 'about' turns NIT to TIN.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut in is to pull sharply in front of another vehicle, a dangerous piece of driving.

clue.text: Exhaust-emitting vehicle brought back gets Green upset

indicators.note: brought back says the vehicle word is turned round

parts.note: a bus is a vehicle with a smoky exhaust
vert is the heraldic word for green

explanation.surface: A smoky bus returns and annoys an environmentalist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green' looks like an environmentalist; it is the heraldic colour VERT. 'brought back' turns BUS into SUB.
explanation.definitionFit: To subvert something is to undermine or overturn it, to upset it.

clue.text: City's little woman's accommodated in stable

definitions.note: the 's reads as is, linking the definition to the wordplay

indicators.note: accommodated in says the first piece is housed within the next

parts.note: sane means mentally stable
Jo is one of the sisters in Little Women, so Jo's

explanation.surface: A town where a young woman's things are kept in a stable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stable' looks like a horse's home; it means mentally steady.
explanation.definitionFit: San Jose is a city in California, and also the capital of Costa Rica.

clue.text: Servant to play truant, finishing early, very weary at the end

indicators.note: finishing early says the word stops before its last letter

parts.note: to skive is British slang for dodging school or work

indicators.note: at the end picks the final letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A servant bunks off early because they are exhausted.
explanation.walkthrough: SKIVE loses its E to give SKIV; then V and Y from the end of 'weary'.
explanation.definitionFit: A skivvy is a British slang word for a lowly household servant who does menial work.

clue.text: Men supply author

parts.note: OR means other ranks, soldiers who are not officers
a well is a source or supply

explanation.surface: Men provide for a writer.
explanation.definitionFit: George Orwell was the English author of Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four.

clue.text: Asiatic tree hit cupola in storm

indicators.note: in storm suggests the letters are blown into disorder

explanation.surface: A tree in Asia strikes a domed roof during a storm.
explanation.definitionFit: Patchouli is an Asian plant of the mint family, the source of a fragrant oil.

clue.text: "Stupid boy" — headless goon

indicators.note: headless says the name loses its first letter

parts.note: Spike Milligan was one of the Goons of the radio comedy The Goon Show

explanation.surface: An insult hurled at a decapitated fool.
explanation.walkthrough: In the British sitcom Dad's Army, Captain Mainwaring calls young Private Pike a stupid boy.
explanation.definitionFit: Private Pike is the character constantly called a stupid boy in the TV comedy Dad's Army.

clue.text: Lake in dangerous wood

indicators.note: in places the letter inside the next word

parts.note: hot can mean dangerous, as with stolen goods

explanation.surface: A lake sits in a perilous forest.
explanation.definitionFit: A holt is an old or poetic word for a wood or copse.

clue.text: See 3
Island that sounds like heaven

indicators.note: that sounds like says the answer is said the same as the next word's synonym

parts.note: the sky is the heavens

explanation.surface: An island with a heavenly-sounding name.
explanation.definitionFit: Skye is the largest island of the Inner Hebrides in Scotland.

clue.text: Girl heard something indicating death

indicators.note: heard says the girl's name is spoken, giving a word with the same sound

parts.note: Nell is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl hears an ominous sign of death.
explanation.definitionFit: A knell is the tolling of a bell to announce a death.

clue.text: Particularly cut off, needing friend

parts.note: to sever is to cut off
an ally is a friend

explanation.surface: Someone cut off from others particularly needs a friend.
explanation.definitionFit: Severally means separately or individually, each in particular.
